data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The 3-of-26 result is a registry-size confound, not evidence about testing in general: the one module with a shown-to-fail-first installation is also the one module where the test-to-mutation ratio is high enough for a guard to have any measurable effect. The ordinarily-guarded modules lose most of their mutations because their guards were not established against an independent rejection set, and the apparent distribution is an artifact of the small number of mutations per module.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the ordinarily-guarded modules each had dozens of mutations and still lost 4/4 to 6/7, the registry-size explanation would fail.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If compile.py had nine mutations and still lost only one, installation order would be a stronger explanation than mutation count.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the same author produced a second repository with pre-installed failure in a module with many mutations and saw a low loss rate, the confound would be weakened.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"A test only appears to constrain when there are enough mutations to distinguish a selective guard from a descriptive one. With one mutation against compile.py, a single shown-to-fail-first installation produces a clean 1-of-9 loss. With four to seven mutations per ordinarily-guarded module, a guard that merely describes the existing code passes nearly all mutations, producing the observed 4/4 to 6/7 losses. The asymmetry is not a property of the tests but of the mutation counts: the one case with pre-installed failure is also the one case where the denominator is small enough for a single selective event to dominate the fraction.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
